overview: TD Bank Group is the sixth-largest bank in North America by assets (~C$2.1 trillion) and the second-largest bank in Canada, serving more than 28 million clients through four segments: Canadian Personal and Commercial Banking, U.S. Retail (U.S. Banking), Wealth Management and Insurance, and Wholesale Banking (TD Securities/TD Cowen). TD reports in Canadian dollars under IFRS with an October 31 fiscal year end and trades on both the TSX and NYSE. The bank is in the midst of a multi-year, regulator-mandated remediation of its U.S. anti-money-laundering (AML) program following a 2024 Global Resolution with U.S. authorities that imposed fines, a guilty plea, and an asset cap on its U.S. banking subsidiaries.

business_model.summary: TD earns net interest income on a ~C$1.0 trillion loan book funded by ~C$1.26 trillion of deposits (Canadian Personal and Commercial Banking and U.S. Retail), fee-based wealth and insurance income (Wealth Management and Insurance), and trading, underwriting and advisory revenue through TD Securities/TD Cowen (Wholesale Banking). Historically, TD also earned equity-method income from its ~10% stake in Charles Schwab, which was fully sold in February 2025; TD retains an ongoing insured deposit account (IDA) sweep agreement with Schwab through 2034 with a US$60 billion floor. Approximately half of revenue is net interest income (recurring, spread-based) and half is fee/trading income, with the Canadian retail/commercial franchise the most stable profit engine and Wholesale Banking/Wealth the more cyclical complements.

revenue_streams.name: Corporate (incl. one-time Schwab gain, balance sheet restructuring)

business_model.customer_type: Diversified: ~16 million Canadian personal/business clients, over 10 million U.S. retail/business customers, over 6 million Canadian wealth/insurance clients, and over 10,000 corporate, government and institutional clients globally in Wholesale Banking
business_model.geographic_mix: Canada is the dominant profit center (Canadian Personal and Commercial Banking, most of Wealth Management and Insurance); the U.S. is the second-largest market via U.S. Retail (branches from Maine to Florida, TD Auto Finance U.S., TD Wealth U.S.) and a sizeable Wholesale Banking/TD Cowen presence; smaller Wholesale Banking operations in Europe and Asia-Pacific.

main_competitors: regional/community banks and credit unions in the U.S. Northeast/Southeast
competitive_position.market_position: Historically a top-2 Canadian retail/commercial bank by market share and a top-10 U.S. retail bank by deposits in its Maine-to-Florida footprint, branded 'America's Most Convenient Bank.' The U.S. Retail franchise is currently constrained in scale by the regulatory asset cap, while the Canadian franchise, Wealth Management/Insurance, and Wholesale Banking (TD Securities/TD Cowen) continue to compete at scale.

moat_factors.description: 1,051 Canadian branches, 3,370 ATMs, and a top-2 position in Canadian retail/commercial banking products benefit from Canada's concentrated 'Big 5/6' bank structure with high regulatory barriers to new entrants.

1,100 U.S. stores and strong brand recognition as 'America's Most Convenient Bank' in the U.S. Northeast/Mid-Atlantic/Southeast, though growth is currently capped by the OCC asset limitation, blunting this advantage versus uncapped peers.

Four complementary segments (Canadian retail/commercial, U.S. retail, Wealth/Insurance, Wholesale) provide some earnings diversification, though U.S. Retail's contribution has been structurally impaired since the 2024 AML resolution.

TD historically ranked highly in JD Power customer satisfaction surveys (digital banking, SBA lending, auto finance dealer satisfaction) in both Canada and the U.S., though brand reputation took a reputational hit from the AML guilty plea and criminal conviction of U.S. subsidiaries.

Combination of TD Securities (Canadian/global capital markets) and the 2023-acquired TD Cowen (U.S. equity research, trading and advisory) creates a broader North American wholesale banking platform generating record revenue in FY2025-2026.

Multi-product retail and commercial relationships (deposits, mortgages, cards, wealth) create moderate switching costs, reinforced by cross-sell between U.S. Retail, TD Securities Middle Market partnerships (OneTD), and Wealth Management.

weaknesses: U.S. Retail segment profitability and growth are directly constrained by the OCC-imposed asset cap (US$434 billion) until the AML remediation program is validated and approved by regulators, likely not before 2027-2028
Reputational damage from a criminal guilty plea by U.S. banking subsidiaries (money laundering conspiracy, inadequate AML controls) is a unique overhang versus Canadian bank peers
Loss of the Charles Schwab equity-method earnings stream (fully divested February 2025) removed a historically profitable, low-capital-intensity U.S. income source
Failed 2022-2023 First Horizon acquisition demonstrated execution/regulatory risk in U.S. expansion ambitions and cost TD a US$225 million break fee without achieving the planned U.S. Southeast scale

Elevated and still-rising U.S. BSA/AML remediation spend (~US$550 million pre-tax expected in fiscal 2026, up from ~US$500 million prior guidance) is a persistent expense drag with an uncertain full completion date

growth_drivers: Completion of U.S. balance sheet restructuring (10%+ asset reduction, ~US$22 billion of non-core loans exited, US$382 billion total U.S. Bank assets as of Oct 2025 vs. the US$434 billion cap) freed up headroom for renewed, disciplined U.S. loan growth starting in fiscal 2026-2027

New enterprise strategy unveiled at September 2025 Investor Day (Deeper Relationships, Simpler & Faster, Disciplined Execution) targeting ~13% adjusted ROE and 6-8% adjusted EPS growth for fiscal 2026, rising to ~16% ROE and 7-10% EPS growth by fiscal 2029, alongside a structural cost-reduction program (efficiency ratio target moving into the mid-50s by FY2029)

Large capital return program funded by the Schwab sale proceeds and strong CET1 (14.3% as of Q3 FY2026): a new share buyback program of up to C$10 billion announced September 2026 (following completion of a C$7 billion NCIB in September 2026), to be completed by July 2027
Record Wholesale Banking performance (TD Securities/TD Cowen) with revenue up 25% YoY and ROE of 16.7% in Q3 FY2026, driven by higher client activity, trading and advisory/underwriting fees

Wealth Management and Insurance momentum: record revenue/earnings, AUM up 23% YoY, mass affluent balances up 21% YoY, new accounts up 26% YoY, supported by investment in financial advisor headcount and digital engagement

AI and digital investment (Layer 6 GenAI R&D center, Gen2 deposit-based underwriting machine-learning models) aimed at improving credit decisioning, productivity and personalization across Canadian and U.S. retail

U.S. Banking recovery trajectory: net income up 41% YoY in Q3 FY2026, ROE up 310 bps YoY to 10.2%, as balance sheet actions conclude and the bank pivots toward middle-market commercial lending, proprietary credit cards, and mass-affluent wealth growth once freed from active restructuring

business.risk: U.S. BSA/AML program remediation execution risk
business.description: The Bank must complete management remediation actions, Suspicious Activity Report lookback reviews (expected to conclude calendar 2027), and pass independent monitor/regulator validation before the asset cap can be lifted; timeline could extend beyond 2027, and further findings could expand scope or costs.

business.risk: U.S. Retail growth constrained by the asset cap
business.description: The US$434 billion combined asset limitation on TD Bank, N.A. and TD Bank USA, N.A. restricts organic U.S. loan/deposit growth and new product/market/store approvals (which require OCC supervisory approval) until the OCC accepts the Bank's improved AML policies and procedures.

TD Bank, N.A. and TD Bank US Holding Company pleaded guilty to conspiracy/AML program failures; this unique criminal history among large North American banks could affect client/counterparty relationships, hiring, and regulatory scrutiny in other jurisdictions (e.g., FINTRAC review of the Enterprise AML Program in Canada).

business.risk: Credit migration in Canadian consumer lending
business.description: PCL rose to $4,506 million in FY2025 (+$253 million YoY), driven by credit migration in Canadian consumer lending portfolios and trade/tariff-related performing provisions; management guided fiscal 2026 total PCL to 40-50 bps of credit volume.

business.risk: Competitive intensity from fintech and non-traditional entrants
business.description: Direct banks, fintechs and private credit institutions are gaining share in both Canadian and U.S. personal/business banking and wealth management, pressuring fee and deposit economics.

financial.description: A meaningful share of U.S. Retail and Wholesale Banking earnings are USD-denominated; CAD/USD moves affect translated revenue and expenses (e.g., FX added $319 million to U.S. Retail reported revenue in FY2025 vs. FY2024).

financial.risk: Net interest income drag from balance sheet restructuring
financial.description: Bond sales and loan portfolio exits to manage the asset cap reduced total Bank net interest income by an estimated US$100 million pre-tax in FY2025 and an expected US$280 million pre-tax in FY2026, even as repositioning generates offsetting NII benefits (US$500-550 million pre-tax).

financial.risk: Elevated remediation and restructuring expense base
financial.description: Adjusted non-interest expenses grew 12% YoY in FY2025, well above the Bank's own 5-7% guided range, driven by governance/control investments (including ~US$507 million of AML remediation costs) and business growth spend; a ~$825 million pre-tax restructuring program is still being completed.

CET1 of 14.3-14.7% is comfortably above OSFI minimums, but large buybacks (up to C$10 billion announced September 2026) funded by one-time Schwab proceeds are not a repeatable capital source once fully deployed.

regulatory.description: TD remains subject to formal independent compliance monitorship, DOJ plea agreement probation (five years, extendable), Board certification requirements for U.S. subsidiary dividends, and the threat of a further 7% mandated asset reduction if the U.S. Bank remains non-compliant with OCC consent order articles in any given year.

regulatory.risk: FINTRAC review of Enterprise AML Program (Canada)
regulatory.description: Following Q1 FY2025, Canada's FINTRAC began reviewing TD's remediation steps for FINTRAC violations; the review is ongoing and could result in additional regulatory actions or penalties in TD's home market.
Effective November 1, 2024, Pillar Two rules have modestly raised TD's effective tax rate (~30 bps impact in FY2025) and could evolve further as more jurisdictions implement the OECD framework.

Elevated enforcement focus on AML across the Canadian and U.S. banking industry (e.g., Canada's Bill C-12) increases compliance costs and penalty risk industry-wide, with TD under heightened scrutiny given its recent history.

macro.risk: U.S. tariff policy and trade disruption
macro.description: TD Economics flags persistent U.S. tariffs, CUSMA renewal uncertainty, and trade-related credit impacts on Canadian PCL (particularly performing provisions) as an ongoing drag on both U.S. and Canadian growth.
Canadian unemployment was 6.9% in October 2025 and forecast to rise to 7.3% by calendar year-end amid soft hiring and slower population growth, pressuring consumer credit quality and mortgage demand.

Bank of Canada cut to 2.25% in October 2025 with rates expected to hold; the U.S. Federal Reserve cut to 3.75-4.00% in October 2025 with further cuts expected toward 3.00-3.25%; NIM, deposit costs and structural hedge income are sensitive to the pace and extent of further moves in both countries.

U.S. consumer spending has slowed, residential investment continues to contract, and unemployment reached a cycle high of 4.4% in September 2025, which could pressure U.S. Retail credit quality and loan demand just as the segment seeks to resume growth.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Canadian GDP growth is expected to remain modest through calendar 2026, aided by lower borrowing costs, government defense/infrastructure spending and a gradual housing recovery, while U.S. growth is expected to reaccelerate above 2% in 2026 as tariff effects fade and rates decline further. The concentrated Canadian banking oligopoly supports stable domestic retail/commercial earnings, while U.S. retail banking is highly competitive and currently constrained for TD specifically by the regulatory asset cap.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate: Canadian Personal and Commercial Banking net interest income is relatively stable, but PCL is cyclical and rising with trade/tariff uncertainty; Wholesale Banking and Wealth Management fee/trading income are more cyclical, tied to market activity, trading volumes and M&A/underwriting cycles; U.S. Retail's near-term trajectory is additionally shaped by the idiosyncratic regulatory remediation timeline rather than the economic cycle alone.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High — NIM (1.82% reported in Q3 FY2026), deposit mix, and loan origination volumes are directly affected by Bank of Canada and U.S. Federal Reserve policy rates; the Schwab IDA sweep deposit agreement (US$60 billion floor) also ties a portion of U.S. deposit-related income to short-term rate levels.
key_input_costs: Staff/compensation costs (largest expense line, >50% of non-interest expense)
U.S. BSA/AML remediation and governance/control investment (~US$550 million guided for FY2026)
Restructuring/severance costs (~$825 million pre-tax program nearing completion)

recent_developments.event: Announced intention to launch a new share buyback program (Normal Course Issuer Bid) to repurchase up to C$10 billion / 61 million common shares, subject to OSFI approval, to be completed by July 2027, following completion of a C$7 billion NCIB on September 25, 2026 (47.2 million shares).

One year after the September 2025 Investor Day, management reported the Bank is ahead of the vast majority of its medium-term targets across all business segments, with CEO Raymond Chun emphasizing 'disciplined execution' and progress on cost restructuring, branch format changes, and hiring ~450 additional client-facing bankers.

Record quarterly results: reported net income $4,615 million (+38% YoY), adjusted diluted EPS $2.77 (+26% YoY), beating consensus; record earnings in Canadian Personal and Commercial Banking and Wholesale Banking (+87% reported net income YoY), and improving U.S. Banking profitability (net income +41% YoY, ROE +310 bps to 10.2%); CET1 ratio 14.3%.

U.S. BSA/AML remediation and governance/control cost guidance for fiscal 2026 raised to ~US$550 million pre-tax (from ~US$500 million previously) due to increased lookback review costs; Suspicious Activity Report lookback reviews required under the OCC consent order still expected to complete in calendar 2027.

Full fiscal year reported net income of $20,538 million (+132% YoY) driven primarily by the $8.6 billion net gain on the Schwab share sale; adjusted net income of $15,025 million (+5% YoY); reported ROE 17.8%; new medium-term financial targets set at the September 2025 Investor Day (~13% adjusted ROE and 6-8% adjusted EPS growth for FY2026, rising to ~16% ROE and 7-10% EPS growth by FY2029).

TD sold its entire remaining 10.1% equity stake in Charles Schwab (184.7 million shares) for proceeds of $21.0 billion (US$14.6 billion), recognizing an $8.6 billion net gain and adding 238 bps to CET1 capital; TD continues the Schwab Insured Deposit Account sweep agreement (through 2034, US$60 billion floor) but no longer records equity-method earnings from Schwab.

Completed U.S. balance sheet restructuring: sold US$31.9 billion of bonds (aggregate pre-tax loss of US$1,592 million) and exited ~US$22 billion of non-core U.S. loans (including a US$9 billion correspondent mortgage portfolio and wind-down of a US$3 billion retail card/point-of-sale business), reducing U.S. Bank combined assets to US$382 billion (from the US$434 billion cap), creating roughly US$52 billion of headroom.

Announced the Global Resolution of U.S. BSA/AML investigations: US$3.088 billion (C$4.233 billion) in penalties to OCC, Federal Reserve, FinCEN and DOJ; guilty pleas by TD Bank, N.A. and TD Bank US Holding Company; imposition of the US$434 billion U.S. Bank asset cap, independent compliance monitorship, and OCC supervisory pre-approval for new U.S. products/markets/stores.

guidance.as_of: Q3 FY2026 Report to Shareholders (August 27, 2026) and FY2025 Annual Report / September 2025 Investor Day

items.notes: Set at the September 2025 Investor Day as part of new Bank-wide targets; medium-term (FY2029) target is ~16% adjusted ROE. Nine-month FY2026 adjusted ROE was 14.8%, running ahead of the full-year target.
Medium-term (FY2029) target is 7-10% adjusted EPS growth. FY2026 YTD adjusted diluted EPS of $7.59 is up 23% YoY, well ahead of the annual target, aided by easier prior-year comparisons.
Operating leverage defined as adjusted revenue growth (net of ISE) minus adjusted expense growth, adjusted for U.S. strategic card partner PCL gross-up.
Actual CET1 was 14.3% as of Q3 FY2026, comfortably above both the FY2026 target and OSFI minimums, supporting the new C$10 billion buyback program.
Q3 FY2026 adjusted payout ratio was 40.2%, within the target range; dividend per share raised to $1.12/quarter in Q3 FY2026 from $1.05 a year earlier.

items.vs_prior: new target (introduced at Sept 2025 Investor Day)
items.notes: Adjusted efficiency ratio (net of ISE) was 58.4% in FY2025 and 55.2% in Q3 FY2026; management targets structural cost reduction to reach the mid-50s by FY2029.
FY2025 PCL ratio was 0.47%; Q3 FY2026 PCL ratio was 0.37% (nine-month FY2026: 0.41%), tracking within or better than the guided range.
Raised due to increased costs associated with Suspicious Activity Report lookback activities required under the OCC consent order; lookback reviews expected to complete in calendar 2027.

items.target: Up to C$10 billion (61 million shares)
items.notes: Announced September 30, 2026, subject to OSFI approval, following completion of a prior C$7 billion NCIB on September 25, 2026; funded in part by residual Schwab sale proceeds and strong organic capital generation.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Raymond Chun characterized Q3 FY2026 as 'a very strong quarter, with record earnings in our Canadian businesses and Wholesale Banking, and growing momentum in U.S. Banking,' emphasizing disciplined execution, positive operating leverage, and continued investment in front-line talent and AI. Management stated the Bank is 'ahead of the vast majority' of the medium-term targets set at the September 2025 Investor Day, one year on, across all business segments. On the AML remediation, management reiterated that significant work and milestones remain through calendar 2027 (including the OCC-mandated Suspicious Activity Report lookback), that timing is not entirely within the Bank's control due to required regulatory approvals and monitor/DOJ review, and that the overall remediation timeline could extend beyond calendar 2027 if additional findings emerge.

bull_case: U.S. balance sheet restructuring is largely complete (US$382 billion of US$434 billion cap as of Oct 2025), positioning U.S. Banking for renewed, disciplined loan growth in fiscal 2027-2028 once the asset cap pressure eases, with U.S. Banking net income already up 41% YoY in Q3 FY2026

New enterprise strategy under CEO Raymond Chun (since Sept 2025 Investor Day) is tracking ahead of medium-term targets across all segments, with a credible path to ~16% adjusted ROE and a mid-50s efficiency ratio by FY2029 via structural cost cuts and AI-driven productivity

Large, well-funded capital return program (up to C$10 billion buyback through July 2027, on top of a completed C$7 billion NCIB) backed by a 14.3% CET1 ratio and residual Schwab sale proceeds, supporting EPS growth independent of top-line momentum

Record, broad-based FY2025/FY2026 performance in Canadian Personal and Commercial Banking and Wholesale Banking (TD Securities/TD Cowen revenue +25% YoY, ROE 16.7% in Q3 FY2026) demonstrates the core franchise remains highly competitive despite the U.S. AML overhang

Dominant, defensible position in Canadian retail/commercial banking (16 million clients, top-2 market share) in a concentrated oligopoly market provides a stable earnings base largely insulated from the U.S. regulatory situation
bear_case: The U.S. BSA/AML remediation program carries multi-year execution risk and is not entirely within TD's control (regulator/monitor/DOJ approval required); the asset cap could persist well into 2027-2028 or be extended further, and a mandated additional 7% U.S. asset reduction is possible if remediation milestones are missed

Reputational and franchise damage from a criminal guilty plea by U.S. banking subsidiaries is unprecedented among large North American banks and could have lasting effects on client trust, talent retention, and regulatory relationships, including an ongoing FINTRAC review of TD's Enterprise AML Program in Canada

Elevated and still-rising remediation/governance spend (~US$550 million guided for FY2026, up from ~US$500 million) combined with adjusted expense growth running well above management's own prior guidance ranges pressures near-term margins and the path to the FY2029 efficiency target

Loss of the historically profitable, low-capital Charles Schwab equity-method income stream (fully divested February 2025) permanently removes a U.S. earnings contributor, leaving U.S. Banking to rebuild profitability largely organically under capped growth constraints

The failed US$13.4 billion First Horizon acquisition (terminated May 2023, US$225 million break fee paid) illustrates execution and regulatory-approval risk in TD's U.S. growth ambitions, and the one-time nature of Schwab-sale-funded buybacks and cost-cutting-driven targets could disappoint if organic revenue growth fails to accelerate once the restructuring tailwinds fade
